BREAKING: US corporate profits before tax as a % of GDP are up to a record 14%.

This ratio has nearly doubled since the 2008 Financial Crisis.

This also exceeds previous peaks of ~13% posted in 1951, 2010, and 2011.

Meanwhile, US corporate profits after tax as a % of GDP are up to ~11%, also an all-time high.

By comparison, this figure averaged ~5% between 1980 and 1995.

This comes as nominal profits after tax have surged +101% since the 2020 pandemic, to a record $3.62 trillion.

US corporations are more profitable than ever.

⚡️BREAKING: 🇺🇦Ukraine purchased 70 M39 ATACMS ballistic missiles, 12 M270 MLRS using GMLRS and ATACMS missiles from Turkey, and tens of thousands of cluster munitions.

This is stated in the reports of the US State Department, published in the official protocol of the work of the US Congress for August 6, 2026.

The transfer is scheduled to begin immediately after the expiry of the statutory deadline for the 15-day review of communications by Congress. The State Department submitted the relevant documents to the legislators on August 3, 2026.

In general, the Congress reported on the transfer to Ukraine:

▪️12 M270 MLRS launchers;
▪️70 M39 ATACMS ballistic missiles;
▪️2524 unguided 227 mm M26 rockets with DPICM cluster warheads;
▪️47,000 M509A1 203 mm caliber cluster artillery shells for 2S7 "Pion" and M110 self-propelled guns.

According to the report, the transfer will be carried out through Turkish, Bulgarian and American defense and logistics companies-special exporters.

The State Department has told Congress that it is ready to allow the transfer because it is in line with U.S. security assistance goals.

The documents state that Turkey seeks to reduce stocks of obsolete weapons in order to focus financial resources on modernizing and maintaining existing systems. Ukraine, in turn, wants to purchase these weapons to strengthen the offensive and defensive capabilities of fire support during the counteraction of the Russian invasion.

The market has seemingly lost faith in memory companies' ability to sustain their earnings beyond next year.

This, amomgst Korean deleveraging, institutional profit taking, and "weaker than expected" Q3 guidance.

Just look at how deeply their forward P/E multiples have compressed:

- Micron: 6.1x
- Sandisk: 5.8x
- Samsung Electronics: 3.7x
- Kioxia: 3.7x
- SK hynix: 3.5x

It now seems like a tapering off of ASPs, and therefore gross margins mean-reverting, is being priced in. In that sense, memory now becomes a revenue play. 

I.e., can the memory vendors supply at an increased rate to fuel their top line, and resulting bottom line, growth? @jukan05 has been alluding to the supply-side recently, but any additional insights are welcome.

One thing that at least remains true is that there is basically no demand-side issue. Almost every infra CEO pointed towards the memory shortages as one of their key growth blockers. From SpaceX to Applied Optoelectronics.

There are other considerations too:

1. We're by no means in a bull market for AI infrastructure. If and when confidence returns, who's to say that memory names won't get re-rated higher even just as a consequence of their high beta? 

2. As @amitisinvesting points out, memory is a short-term trade rather than a secular compounder like Palantir. So, are retail and institutions just done with the memory trade at this point?

These are purposely conflicting questions which I believe each individual investor should work through independently.

One of the biggest public bulls on memory just sold all his memory stocks. 

This is quite interesting. For the past few months, if you mentioned anything bearish on memory without having a position (short or long) the comments from people who seemingly got on the train at $700-$800 would decimate you.

“You missed the run. You don’t get it. You’re jealous.”

Instead of actively engaging with some basic bear cases (memory optimization, prices peaking, supply coming online) you just got pushback. Even if you’d say that buybacks aren’t really a strategy on what to do with excess cash…you’d be labeled as someone who doesn’t understand why buybacks are good. As if Apple buying back their stock with sustainable growth is the same as a commodity supplier in the greatest supply/demand imbalance we have ever seen doing buybacks as well?

I personally believe $MU probably has a fair value closer to $1500, but if the broader market has external concerns that discount those future cashflows, then obviously that can hurt the potential for that price action.

I am not bearish, not short, just on the sidelines because I missed the run and didn’t want to chase. The bulls not willing to even hear the bear case is one again a reminder that when a group of people ignore anything that could deter the thesis, it tends to be a red flag. 

Having said that, Hynix and Samsung can’t go down. If they do, Korea is done. I think this would be bad for US stocks. Would really like to not see that because I have high beta exposure and would like US memory stocks to do well because many other semi names follow those names.

My biggest issue is whenever I ask people if they are in memory stocks for a trade or an investment, literally 99% say it’s a trade. No one wants to hold for 5 years. 

If so, then that means there is really doubt on the sustainability of those earnings which is what the market may be thinking right now.

I do feel like much of the fear is priced in and hopefully a short term bounce is near but it would require momentum to come back into these names.
